chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
“My house is assessed at such-and-such by the city.” You hear this phrase often — and it leads to many misunderstandings about prices. The municipal assessment and market value are two different things, with two distinct uses.

This guide clarifies the difference, explains the comparative factor, and helps you use the right number at the right time.

Each chapter ends with a lined “My notes” page.

“My house is assessed at such-and-such by the city”: this phrase leads to many misunderstandings. This guide clarifies the difference between the municipal assessment (a tax tool) and market value (the market price), explains the comparative factor and how to contest an assessment.

The key message: the right number at the right time.

chapters.title: The municipal assessment: a tax tool
chapters.html:
Understanding what it's really for.

The municipal assessment appears on the assessment roll. Its purpose isn't to set a sale price: it serves to allocate the taxes, municipal and school.

It's established “in bulk”, at a reference date, for an entire territory — not property by property at today's price. As a result:

  • It can be higher or lower than the real market value.
  • It often lags in time.

The municipal assessment appears on the assessment roll and serves to allocate the taxes. Established in bulk, at a reference date, with a lag, it can be higher or lower than the market. “The city assesses it at such-and-such, so that's what it's worth” is the number-one misunderstanding.

Emilie's tip

“The city assesses it at such-and-such, so that's what it's worth”: that's the number-one misunderstanding. The municipal assessment is used to calculate your taxes, not to set the sale price.

chapters.title: Market value: the market price
chapters.objective: Understanding what a buyer actually pays.
chapters.html:
Understanding what a buyer actually pays.

Market value is the price an informed buyer is ready to pay today, under current market conditions.

It's determined by a comparative market analysis (recent sales of similar properties), not by the assessment roll.

It's this number — and it alone — that should guide a sale price or a purchase offer.

Market value is the price an informed buyer pays today, determined by a comparative analysis (recent similar sales) — not by the roll. It's this number, and it alone, that should guide a sale price or a purchase offer.

Emilie's tip

To know the real value of your property, ask for a comparative analysis based on recent sales in the area. It's the only number that counts when it's time to sell or buy.

chapters.title: The comparative factor and the right uses
chapters.html:
Linking the two concepts correctly.

The municipality applies a comparative factor to try to bring the assessment roll closer to market value — for example in calculating the Welcome Tax.

This clearly shows that the assessment alone isn't the market value. To each number its use:

  • Municipal assessment: for the taxes, and as the (adjusted) basis of the Welcome Tax.
  • Market value: to set a price, make an offer, negotiate.

The municipality applies a comparative factor to bring the roll closer to the market (notably for the Welcome Tax), which clearly shows that the assessment alone isn't the market value. To each number its use: assessment for the taxes, market value to set a price.

Emilie's tip

To estimate your Welcome Tax, remember that the higher of the price paid and the municipal assessment adjusted by the comparative factor is used. It avoids nasty surprises.

chapters.title: Contesting your municipal assessment
chapters.objective: Acting if the roll seems wrong to you.
chapters.html:
Acting if the roll seems wrong to you.

If your municipal assessment seems clearly too high relative to the market, you can contest it — within a specific deadline following the filing of a new roll.

  1. Compare your assessment to that of similar properties.
  2. Gather proof (comparable sales, the building's real condition).
  3. File a request for review with the municipality within the provided deadline.

Too high an assessment can inflate your taxes year after year: it can be worth the effort.

If your assessment seems clearly too high relative to the market, you can contest it within a specific deadline following the filing of a new roll: compare with similar properties, gather proof and file a request for review. Too high an assessment inflates your taxes for years.

Emilie's tip

Don't miss the review deadline. If your assessment clearly exceeds that of comparable houses, a well-documented challenge can reduce your taxes for years.

chapters.title: The right number at the right time
chapters.html:
Never confusing the two again.

In practice, keep this simple reflex depending on the situation:

  • I'm selling or making an offer → market value (comparative analysis).
  • I'm checking my taxes → municipal assessment (the roll).
  • I'm estimating my Welcome Tax → the higher of the price paid or the adjusted assessment.

Both numbers are useful; it's mixing them up that leads to pricing errors.

Keep this reflex: I'm selling or offering → market value; I'm checking my taxes → municipal assessment; I'm estimating my Welcome Tax → the higher of the price paid or the adjusted assessment. Both numbers are useful; it's mixing them up that leads to pricing errors.

Emilie's tip

Picture two mental drawers: “taxes” for the municipal assessment, “price” for market value. Never reach into the wrong drawer when it's time to negotiate.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Find my municipal assessment and its date.
  2. Ask for a comparative analysis for the market value.

Within 30 days

  1. Use market value for any pricing decision.
  2. Understand the comparative factor for the Welcome Tax.

Next

  1. Stop confusing the two numbers.

Good reflexes

  1. Use market value (comparative analysis) for any pricing decision.
  2. Check the challenge deadline if my assessment clearly exceeds the market.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Assessment roll: the municipal register of values, the basis for taxes.
  • Municipal assessment: a tax value, distinct from the sale price.
  • Market value: the price an informed buyer pays today.
  • Comparative factor: a coefficient bringing the assessment closer to the market.
  • Comparative analysis: recent sales used to determine market value.
  • Assessment roll: the municipal register of values, the basis for taxes.
  • Municipal assessment: a tax value, distinct from the sale price.
  • Market value: the price an informed buyer pays today.
  • Comparative factor: a coefficient bringing the assessment closer to the market.
  • Request for review: the recourse to contest an assessment.

qcm.q: The municipal assessment mainly serves to:

options: A) At today's price, property by property
B) In bulk, at a reference date
B) The price an informed buyer pays today
B) Bring the assessment closer to the market (e.g. Welcome Tax)

qcm.q: To set a sale price, you use:
Too high a municipal assessment can:
options: B) Inflate your taxes year after year
D) Be ignored with no effect
B) File a request for review within the provided deadline

qcm.q: To check your taxes, the right number is:
options: C) The price paid by the neighbour

qcm.q: The Welcome Tax is based on:
options: A) The lower of the two numbers
B) The higher of the price paid or the adjusted assessment
qcm.explanation: The higher of the two (ch. 3 and 5).
